---
title: "Reticence: Reading Probability Backwards"
---

“One chance in six” can be read from either end.

The fraction $1/6$ describes the share of trials that produce an event under the model. The number six gives a scale on which to think about repeated opportunities.

This change of viewpoint makes reciprocal probability a useful bridge.

## 🏵 A proposed name with an explicit definition {#sec-sample-reticence-a-proposed-name-with-an-explicit-definition}

In this book, let **reticence** be a working name for

$$
\mathcal R(A)=\frac1{\mathbb P(A)},
\qquad \mathbb P(A)>0.
$$

The established mathematical description is *reciprocal event probability*. The name is a conceptual aid, not a claim that a generator has intentions or physically opposes an outcome.

For a fair die:

- A six has probability $1/6$ and reticence $6$.
- An even face has probability $1/2$ and reticence $2$.
- A face in $\{1,\ldots,6\}$ has probability one and reticence one.

As an event becomes less likely, its reticence grows. For an event of zero probability, we may use $+\infty$ as an extended-value convention; ordinary division by zero remains undefined.

“Resistance” suggests a physical mechanism. “Reticence” gives us a looser metaphor while leaving the mathematical quantity unchanged. Neither name determines which reciprocal was intended; the equation does.

## 🔰 When does it count attempts? {#sec-sample-reticence-when-does-it-count-attempts}

Repeat independent trials, each with the same success probability $p>0$. Let $T$ count trials up to and including the first success.

Call the expected number of trials $m$. We always spend one trial. With probability $1-p$ we fail and face the same waiting problem again:

$$
m=1+(1-p)m.
$$

Therefore,

$$
m=\frac1p.
$$

This is the mean of the geometric waiting-time distribution. Reticence has an operational interpretation here: **the expected number of attempts, including the successful one**.

It is an average across repeated runs. It does not promise success by attempt $\mathcal R$.

For the six on a fair die, the mean wait is six rolls. As [Dice and Decks](dice-and-decks.qmd) showed, the chance of seeing at least one six by then is only about $0.665$.

## ⚙️ Several quantities can sound like “the opposite” {#sec-sample-reticence-several-quantities-can-sound-like-the-opposite}

For $p=1/6$, distinguish these readings:

- **Complement probability:** $1-p=5/6$, the chance of no six on one roll.
- **Reticence:** $1/p=6$, the reciprocal probability.
- **Odds against:** $(1-p)/p=5$, five units of failure weight per unit of success weight.
- **Surprise:** $-\log_2p=\log_2 6\approx2.585$ bits.

Under the independent repeated-trial model, odds against also equal the expected number of failures before the first success. They are $\mathcal R-1$.

Surprise takes a logarithm of reticence:

$$
I(A)=\log_2\mathcal R(A).
$$

For independent events, probabilities multiply, reticences multiply, and surprises add. Two independent sixes have probability $1/36$, reticence $36$, and surprise $2\log_2 6$ bits. This is a first bridge to [Shannon's information-theoretic scale](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf).

## ⚠️ The waiting interpretation belongs to a procedure {#sec-sample-reticence-the-waiting-interpretation-belongs-to-a-procedure}

A shuffled six-card deck has first-draw probability $1/6$ for its six. But its position is equally likely to be $1,2,\ldots,6$, giving mean position

$$
\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6}=3.5.
$$

The initial reciprocal probability is still six. It is not the mean wait in this changing-inventory procedure.

Reticence also belongs to an event. In a continuous model, even a possible exact value can have probability zero; a finite-resolution question should specify an interval. Taking the reciprocal of a continuous density would produce a quantity with units that changes under a change of coordinates. For finite-resolution observations, first calculate an interval probability.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-reticence-try-the-idea}

An event has probability $1/4$. Give its reticence, complement probability, odds against, and surprise. Which quantity counts failed attempts on average under independent repetition?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-reticence-work-it-through}

The values are $4$, $3/4$, $3$, and $2$ bits. Odds against, $3$, count failures on average under the stated repeated-trial model. Reticence, $4$, also includes the final successful attempt.
:::
